title: Flathub bans AI-coded apps – with some exceptions
content:
You’ll have to sift through fewer vibe-coded apps on Flathub in future, as the store has announced a policy change on software made using AI tools.
Flathub, the de-facto place to find and install Flatpak applications, is banning the use of “AI” coded applications and automated submissions going forward.
A change to the store’s policy note says “applications containing AI-generated or AI-assisted code, documentation, or other content are not allowed”.
A carve out will allow “mature, well-maintained projects” to include AI generated code and use AI tools for generating and handling submissions.
Existing AI-coded apps available on Flathub are also exempt (which will be music to the ears of the Amberol-alikes, I’m sure).
Flathub’s Bart Piotrowski explained more on the reason behind the policy on Mastodon, citing negative experiences with “entitled submitters acting as if they were bestowing their brilliant software upon us idiots who are rejecting it”.
But they also note their own reservations in committing to banning vibe-coded software, feeling that “LLMs are inevitable”.
‘Depressing’ amount of slop submissions
Submissions to Flathub are handled via GitHub pull requests. Under the new policy, no part of that process can be automated using AI tools or agents, including the manifest, metadata, patches, build scripts and the PR itself.
A Cursor-y1 glance at Flathub’s current submission queue shows a depressing sludge of vibecoded projects angling for inclusion on the store.
Curtailing automated submissions at the root is simply a pragmatic move. Plugging the slopportunity hole should help prevent an ever-scaling influx of low-effort, low-passion identikit-projects that clog volunteer-led approval and review processes.
More pointedly, it could also reduce the amount of chaff the store has to host (infrastructure isn’t cheap) which means users are more likely to find good-quality software.
The majority of low-effort vibe coded apps are spur-of-the-moment clones or riffs on existing tools and lack evidence of commitment2 to maintenance or a vision. Developers of vibeware still have other distribution avenues, like the Snap Store.
A case of “if you couldn’t be bothered to code or submit it, we can’t be bothered to review or host it”.
The crux of the policy change will be in how “exceptions” to the revised policy are handled, since it won’t apply retroactively to existing apps on the store.
Piotrowski says community engagement, release cadence and continuous integration systems – i.e., indications that it isn’t one-shot slopware® made on a whim – will be the bar against which exceptions are viewed.
Cue the tokenburn from AI agents being asked to generate an app, icon, documentation, website, manifest AND now a slew of community simulacrum too…

report.summary: Flathub now bans apps made with AI-generated code and automated submissions, but exempts existing apps and mature projects that prove genuine maintenance.
report.background: Flathub is the main store for Flatpak Linux apps, maintained largely by volunteers. Concerned about a wave of low-effort 'vibe-coded' apps created with LLM tools, it introduced a rule banning AI-generated or AI-assisted code, documentation, or other content. It also bars automating any part of the GitHub submission process. Moderator Bart Piotrowski said entitled submitters and a queue full of slop prompted the move, and that infrastructure and review time are limited. Existing apps are exempt, and mature, well-maintained projects may still use AI tools if they demonstrate ongoing commitment through regular releases and community engagement.
key_points: Under the new policy, Flathub will reject applications that contain AI-generated or AI-assisted code, documentation, or other content. It also forbids using AI agents to automate any part of the Flatpak submission process, including pull requests, manifests, metadata, patches, and build scripts.

Flathub says the move is a response to a flood of low-effort, 'vibe-coded' apps in its submission queue. Volunteer moderators faced entitled developers who expected acceptance, while reviewing endless clones drained time and bandwidth. Banning AI submissions at the root is meant to stop the influx of identikit projects.

Existing apps on Flathub are grandfathered and won't be removed. Mature, well-maintained projects can also get exceptions and still use AI-generated code or AI-assisted tooling. To qualify, a project must demonstrate community engagement, a reliable release cadence, and continuous integration systems, rather than looking like a one-shot app made on a whim.

The ban aims to improve discoverability and maintain user trust by cutting down on chaff. Flathub doesn't just review pull requests; it hosts and serves apps, so every accepted submission has real infrastructure and moderation costs. Larger app stores may face similar pressure as generative AI makes cheap clones easier to produce.
Developers of low-effort AI-generated apps still have other distribution avenues, such as the Snap Store, but they cannot expect Flathub's volunteer reviewers to host and maintain their slopware.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Flathub’s move signals a correction after the initial hype of generative coding: distribution platforms are beginning to filter for long-term maintenance rather than raw code generation. Developers who use AI assistants as part of a serious workflow can still pass the bar if they show consistent releases and community interaction, but casual 'vibe-code and submit' workflows face a closed door. Regular users should see fewer redundant clones and an easier time finding quality Linux apps. The policy is also a reminder that automated submissions create invisible labor for volunteer reviewers; expect other curated ecosystems to consider similar quality-based AI policies.
report.tools: Readers who want to see how Flatpak submissions are vetted can explore Flathub’s GitHub repository and the official flatpak-builder tool. flatpak-builder-lint can validate app metadata before submission, and studying well-maintained Flatpak apps on Flathub offers practical examples of how mature projects structure manifests and releases.
